docs.title: Data & Metrics Glossary
docs.text:
Welcome to this structured reference for data concepts, metrics, and terminology.

This glossary is designed to help technical and non-technical teams understand:

  • What each metric means
  • How it is calculated
  • Who uses it and why
  • How it relates to other concepts

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Metrics — definitions and calculation logic for key performance indicators
  • Glossary — core data and technical terminology explained clearly

Maintained by Taimaa Saleh — Computer Engineer & Ontology Researcher

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Core terminology for data, metrics, and analytics concepts.

docs.title: Active User
docs.text:
A user who performs at least one meaningful action within a defined time period (daily, weekly, or monthly).

Related metrics: Engagement Rate

docs.title: Cohort
docs.text:
A group of users who share a common starting point — typically their first use of a product within the same time window.

Cohort analysis tracks how different groups behave over time, making it possible to compare retention across periods.

Related metrics: Retention Rate

docs.title: Churn Rate
docs.text:
The percentage of users who stop using a product within a given period.

$$ \text{Churn Rate} = 100 - \text{Retention Rate} $$

High churn indicates users are not finding sustained value.

docs.title: Data Catalog
docs.text:
A structured inventory of an organization's data assets — including datasets, metrics, pipelines, and their relationships.

A good data catalog answers three questions: - What data exists? - What does it mean? - Who owns it?

docs.title: Metric
docs.text:
A quantifiable measurement used to evaluate performance, behavior, or system state against a defined goal.

A well-defined metric always includes: - A clear definition - A calculation method - An owner - A known limitation

docs.title: Ontology
docs.text:
A formal representation of concepts within a domain and the relationships between them.

In data systems, ontologies provide the semantic layer that makes data interpretable across teams and tools — defining not just what something is called, but what it means.

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
A single continuous period of user activity within a product, bounded by inactivity or logout.

Session length and depth are common inputs to engagement calculations.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
The formal structure that defines how data is organized — field names, types, relationships, and constraints.

Schemas are the contract between data producers and data consumers.

docs.title: What Is an Ontology?
docs.text:
An ontology is a formal representation of concepts within a domain and the relationships between them.

It answers three fundamental questions: - What things exist in this domain? - What are they called — and what do those names actually mean? - How do they relate to each other?

In everyday language, a database tells you that something exists. An ontology tells you what it means.

docs.title: Why Ontologies Matter for Data Systems
docs.text:
Modern data ecosystems face a common problem: the same concept gets called different things by different teams — or different concepts share the same name.

For example: - Is an "active user" someone who logged in today? This week? Who completed a core action? - Is "revenue" gross or net? Before or after refunds?

Without a shared, formal definition, every team answers differently. Ontologies solve this by making definitions explicit, structured, and machine-readable.

docs.title: Ontology vs. Schema vs. Taxonomy
docs.text:
Concept What it defines Example Schema Structure of data Table: users(id, name, email) Taxonomy Hierarchy of categories Animals → Mammals → Dogs Ontology Concepts + relationships + rules "A Customer is a Person who has completed at least one Transaction"

An ontology is the most expressive of the three — it captures not just structure, but meaning and logic.

docs.title: Connection to Data Catalogs
docs.text:
A data catalog without ontological grounding is just a list. A well-structured catalog answers:

  • What is this dataset? (definition)
  • How does it relate to other datasets? (relationships)
  • Who owns it and who uses it? (governance)
  • What does each field actually mean? (semantics)

This is exactly what ontology engineering provides — and why organizations like JetBrains, Google, and the BBC have invested in knowledge graphs and formal vocabularies to power their data infrastructure.

docs.title: My Research Direction
docs.text:
I am preparing for PhD-level research in ontology and knowledge representation, with a focus on:

  • How natural language can be used to extract formal ontological models
  • The role of foundational ontologies (such as UFO — Unified Foundational Ontology) in ensuring semantic consistency across domains
  • How structured vocabularies improve data discoverability and reuse in large-scale data ecosystems

This glossary is a practical expression of that interest — every term here is documented not just as a definition, but as a concept with relationships, scope, and context.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Engagement rate measures how actively users interact with a product, feature, or content within a defined time period.

It indicates whether users find value in what they are using — not just that they opened it, but that they did something meaningful with it.

docs.title: How It Is Calculated
docs.text:
$$ \text{Engagement Rate} = \frac{\text{Active Interactions}} {\text{Total Sessions}} \times 100 $$

Active interactions include:

  • Clicks on core features
  • Time spent above a minimum threshold
  • Actions completed (searches, exports, shares)

docs.title: Who Uses This Metric
docs.text: Team Purpose Product Evaluate feature adoption Data Build usage models Marketing Measure campaign effectiveness

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Retention rate measures the percentage of users who return to a product after their first visit within a defined time window.

It is one of the most critical indicators of long-term product health — acquisition brings users in, retention keeps them.

docs.title: How It Is Calculated
docs.text:
$$ \text{Retention Rate} = \frac{\text{Users who returned}} {\text{Total users at start of period}} \times 100 $$

Common retention windows:

  • Day 1, Day 7, Day 30
  • Weekly cohorts
  • Monthly active users (MAU)

docs.title: Who Uses This Metric
docs.text: Team Purpose Product Identify drop-off points Data Build cohort analysis models Leadership Measure product-market fit
